body_markdown:
Adjusting from a large home to a smaller space is difficult, but can be done if you choose items to take with you with discernment, store items not needed often, and part with items that are not useful. If you make a plan before you move, sort items before packing, and use storage strategically, you can create a functional home without crowding every closet, corner, and walkway.


Moving into a smaller home, apartment, condo, or townhouse often requires a different approach to furniture, décor, clothing, and household supplies. Focus on what supports your daily routine, then donate, recycle, gift, store, or put away the rest.


## Key Takeaways


- Adjusting from a large home to a smaller space starts with determining the items you need for your daily routine and taking only them along with you.
- An important next step is to cull your belongings before packing and keeping necessary items, then sorting the rest into categories like items to donate, recycle, gift, and store.
- To know what will fit in your new space, map your new layout, measure larger furniture, and decide what items are necessary and will fit in the space.
- Use your space creatively; make use of vertical storage, closed cabinets, shelving, and furniture with built-in storage to stay organized in a smaller home without clutter.
- Consider utilizing a self-storage unit as additional storage to keep items that do not fit your new space or daily routine like seasonal clothing, décor, extra furniture, and hobby equipment.


## Determine What Supports Your Daily Routine


**Determining what supports your daily routine helps you decide what belongs in your smaller home.** Start with the items you use regularly, such as daily clothing, kitchen supplies, work materials, seating, and bedroom furniture.


Ask these questions as you sort:


- Do I use this item every week?
- Does this item fit the new layout?
- Does it serve more than one purpose?
- Do I have another item that serves the same function?
- Do I want to display or use it right now?


Focus first on the belongings that support daily life; a smaller space works best when it reflects your current routine. Don’t attempt to stuff everything from your previous home into a smaller space; clutter makes a small space feel even smaller.


## Cull Belongings Before Packing


**Reducing the number of items to be moved before packing reduces the number of boxes, furniture pieces, and household items you move.** Work through one room at a time, and avoid shifting clutter from one area to another.


Sort belongings into these categories:


**Category & Purpose** **What To Do**


Keep Pack items that fit your new home and daily routine


Donate Set aside usable items for a local organization


Recycle Follow local recycling guidance for eligible materials


Gift Share items with friends, family members, or neighbors


Store Pack away items you plan to use later but do not need every day


This culling process helps create a clearer inventory before moving day. It also gives you time to pack more intentionally instead of bringing every item into a smaller home and sorting later; it’s easier to add to your new home thoughtfully than to have to continue to remove items.


## Map the New Layout Before Moving


**Mapping the new layout before moving helps you determine which furniture and belongings will fit in your smaller space.** Request a floor plan, take measurements during a walkthrough, or measure rooms after you receive access to the new home. Then measure doorways, stairwells, elevators, hallways, and room dimensions. Compare those measurements with each furniture piece before moving it.


Measure large furniture first, including:


- Sofas and sectionals
- Dining tables and chairs
- Beds and bedframes
- Dressers and nightstands
- Bookshelves and cabinets
- Desks and office chairs
- Exercise equipment
- Storage furniture


Consider each piece and what function(s) it serves; multipurpose items are very useful when working with a small space.


**Space & Item** **Measurement To Check**


Living Room & Sofa Wall length, sofa width, pathways, and door clearance


Bedroom & Bedframe Room size, wall space, closet access, and walking space


Dining Area & Table Table dimensions, chair clearance, and traffic flow


Entryway & Storage Furniture Door swing, walkway width, and space for everyday items


Home Office & Desk Work surface size, outlet placement, and chair clearance


Keeping doors, walkways, and frequently used areas clear makes a smaller home easier to use.


## Use Vertical & Closed Storage


**Using vertical and closed storage helps you organize a smaller home without filling floors and surfaces with clutter.** Tall bookcases, wall-mounted cabinets, floating shelves, hooks, and pegboards use wall space while keeping walkways open.


Use these space-saving strategies:


- Add shelving above desks, laundry machines, or work surfaces.
- Choose storage cabinets with doors for items you do not want on display.
- Use under-bed containers for clean, dry seasonal clothing or linens.
- Select ottomans, benches, and coffee tables with built-in storage.
- Install hooks for bags, hats, outerwear, and frequently used items.
- Group similar items together in designated zones.
- Don’t forget about ceiling storage!


Closed storage helps contain smaller household items, while open shelving creates room for books, décor, and daily-use supplies. A combination of both adds structure without removing personality from your space.


## Use Self-Storage for Overflow Items


**Using self-storage unit for items that do not fit your smaller living space helps you keep your home focused on your everyday routine and avoid unneeded clutter.** Pack away seasonal clothing and décor, extra furniture, rarely used hobby equipment, and other household items you plan to use later or do not need on a regular basis.


A self-storage unit gives you extra room without forcing immediate decisions about what to do with everything you own. Store items you want to rotate back into your home as your needs, hobbies, or seasons change, or even to keep items that you haven’t decided if you want to keep or not; consider keeping a space of the unit that is reserved for items you’re still considering.


Once you know how much you’ll want to move to a separate space, picking a unit size to fit your needs is easy with Public Storage’s resources on its website. Simply start by measuring your larger furniture and oversized items first, then count bins and boxes, and finally visit the[Public Storage Size Guide](https://www.publicstorage.com/size-guide) to compare unit sizes.


**Unit Size & Typical Use** **Storage Fit**


**5′ x 5′** Seasonal clothing, décor, hobby supplies, and smaller bins


**5′ x 10′** Boxes, small furniture, and items from one room


**10′ x 10′** Furniture, boxes, and household items from several rooms


**10′ x 15′ or Larger** Extra furniture and belongings from a larger downsizing project


## Organize Your Storage Unit for Quick & Easy Access


When you move to small home from a large one and choose to use a storage unit for overflow items, you will very likely visit your storage space often and will want to access your belongings quickly. **Organizing your storage unit thoughtfully helps you retrieve belongings without unpacking the entire space or doing gymnastics over furniture and boxes.** Label bins by room, category, season, etc. and group similar items together.


Use this layout:


- Place larger furniture and shelving units (if necessary) along the walls.
- Leave a clear aisle from the entrance to the back wall.
- Put heavier boxes and bins on the floor, then stack lighter bins on top or on shelving.
- Keep items you expect to retrieve first and/or most often near the entrance.
- Keep an inventory list and a basic map of the unit.


A detailed inventory and clear aisle support easier seasonal swaps and future room updates.


For larger furniture and heavier boxes, consider a unit with[Drive-Up Access](https://www.publicstorage.com/self-storage/drive-up-storage) . Drive-Up Access also allows you to drive your vehicle right up to your ground-level unit, so if you’ll be visiting often to rotate seasonal items in storage, picking up your hobby items, or snagging your sporting equipment on the way out to recreate, it adds convenience. More than 45% of Public Storage’s 4,600 properties across 42 states offer Drive-Up Access facilities.


## Frequently Asked Questions


**How Do I Decide What to Keep When Moving to a Smaller Home?**


When you are downsizing your space, try to identify the items you use regularly and measure your space and furniture to determine if each item fits your new layout. Sort everything else into categories–donate, recycle, gift, and store are good options.


**How Do I Know If My Furniture Will Fit in My New Space?**


To know if your furniture will fit in your new, smaller space by first measuring the space (measuring rooms, doorways, hallways, elevators, and stairwells) to know what space you have to work with. Then measure your furniture–large furniture first, then. Map furniture placement before moving day to preserve clear paths and everyday living space.


**How Can I Create More Useful Storage in a Small Home?**


You can create more storage in a small home by using vertical space for shelving and hooks, wall-mounted cabinets, closed storage, under-bed containers, and furniture with built-in storage. A storage unit for your overflow items helps keep your space free of clutter; more clutter in a room makes it feel smaller.


**What Should I Put in a Self-Storage Unit When Downsizing?**


When you move into a smaller space, put off-season clothing and décor, extra furniture pieces, hobby or sporting equipment, and other household items that do not fit into your daily routine in a self-storage unit.


**What Size Self-Storage Unit Do I Need When Moving to a Smaller Space?**


The right storage unit size for you will depend on:


- What item(s) you’re storing
- The quantity of item(s) you’re storing
- How much extra space you’ll need if you want to access your items while in storage


To find a full guide to help you choose the correct size storage unit for your overflow items after moving from a large home to a smaller space, visit the[Public Storage Size Guide](https://www.publicstorage.com/size-guide) .
